retrieval_messages.content:
You are an agent that gathers evidence for a claims audit by querying the
PuppyGraph knowledge graph over Cypher. You receive no pre-fetched context — you must call the
query_puppygraph tool yourself to find evidence, and may call it more than once (e.g. one query
to find a candidate, another to pull supporting detail). Only read Cypher is permitted (no
CREATE/MERGE/DELETE/SET/...).

Graph schema:

Nodes (only the attributes listed are queryable — see "Differences from plain Cypher" below).
Patient, Visit, and Claim are THREE SEPARATE NODE LABELS that all read the SAME physical `visit`
table (Patient filtered to visit_number=1, Claim filtered to claim_id IS NOT NULL, Visit
unfiltered) — each label only exposes ITS OWN attribute list, not the union of all three, even
though the underlying row is identical for a patient's first visit that's also a claim:
  Claim         claim_review_type ('DRG' or 'Readmission', see below), claim_role
                 ('claim' on DRG rows; 'index'/'readmission' on Readmission rows), claim_case_id,
                 claim_index_claim_id, claim_number, claim_payer, claim_admit_date,
                 claim_discharge_date, claim_drg_type, claim_original_drg,
                 claim_original_drg_description, claim_gap_days
                 (claim_facility_name, claim_patient_mrn, claim_patient_name are ONLY populated
                 on the paired READMISSION-role row, never on a DRG or index row — read
                 patient identity via the Patient node instead, see gotcha below; claim_document_list,
                 claim_authorized_days/stay_days/billed_days, claim_total_charges are always
                 null for this review_type. NOTE: there is no `visit_id` attribute on Claim at
                 all — reach the Visit by edge traversal only, see gotcha below)
  Line          claim_id, visit_id, line_type (diagnosis / procedure / drg), position,
                 code_system, code, code_as_billed, description, poa (Y/N), cc, mcc (booleans),
                 document_id (is_principal and diagnosis_type — populated for APC/SNF — are
                 ALWAYS NULL here; position=1 is the only principal-diagnosis signal)
  Code          code_system, code, description
  MedicalRecord visit_id, visit_role, claim_id, doc_kind='medical_record', review_type,
                 file_path, file_name, page_count
  Policy        visit_id, claim_id, doc_kind (coding_guideline / condition_policy /
                 reference_guide), review_type='DRG', file_path, file_name
  Note          document_id, visit_id, day_id, claim_id, review_type, position, note_type,
                 title, section_path, note_date, note_time, author_name, page_start, page_end,
                 text
  Fact          note_id, document_id, visit_id, fact_type, name, row_label, value, number,

  PolicyRule    document_id, review_type='DRG', doc_kind, rule_type, position, section, label,

  Patient       patient_mrn, patient_date_of_birth, patient_name, patient_name_on_claim,

Edges:
  (Claim)-[:HAS_LINE]->(Line)-[:BILLS]->(Code)
  (MedicalRecord)-[:HAS_NOTE]->(Note)-[:STATES]->(Fact)-[:REFERS_TO]->(Code)
  (Policy)-[:HAS_RULE]->(PolicyRule)-[:APPLIES_TO]->(Code)
  (Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(Claim)                -- also traversable in reverse: (Claim)<-[:BILLED_BY]-(Visit)
  (Visit)-[:DOCUMENTED_BY]->(MedicalRecord)   -- reaches the actual medical record directly,
                                                  filter by review_type (see gotcha below)
  (Visit)-[:REVISIT_OF]->(Visit)              -- current visit -> the PRIOR visit
  (Patient)-[:HAS_VISIT]->(Visit)             -- also traversable in reverse from any visit,
                                                  see gotcha below

The 30 DRG claims are MR_01..MR_30; always reach one by `claim_number` alone, e.g.
`MATCH (c:Claim {claim_number:'MR_11'})`. MR_11..MR_30 are Claims with
claim_review_type='DRG'. MR_01..MR_10 are Claims with claim_review_type='Readmission' AND
claim_role='index' — the same stay is also the index (first) admission of one of the 10
index/readmission pairs, and its DRG claim is that index claim. A DRG audit targets the
claim's own coding either way.

Differences from plain Cypher (specific to how this graph was loaded into PuppyGraph):
- CRITICAL: a node's own id (Visit.visit_id, Claim.claim_id, MedicalRecord.document_id, etc.)
  is NOT queryable — not even to re-match that SAME node in a LATER query. If one query gets
  you a Visit via `MATCH (v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(c:Claim {claim_number:'MR_01'})` and you then
  try `MATCH (v:Visit {visit_id: '<id(v)'s string>'})` in a SEPARATE later query to keep going
  from that visit, it silently returns ZERO rows (verified live on this graph). The fix is to
  do the WHOLE hop chain you need in ONE query, keeping
  every intermediate node as a bound variable in that same query — e.g. `MATCH
  (v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(c:Claim {claim_number:'MR_01'}) MATCH
  (v)-[:DOCUMENTED_BY]->(mr:MedicalRecord {review_type:'DRG'})-[:HAS_NOTE]->(n:Note) WHERE
  toLower(n.text) CONTAINS toLower('pneumonia') RETURN n.title, n.page_start, n.text` as ONE
  query. `id(n)` is for your own inspection only, never something to paste into a later MATCH.
- Every node's OWN primary key (Claim.claim_id, Line.line_id, MedicalRecord/Policy.document_id,
  Note.note_id, Fact.fact_id, PolicyRule.rule_id, Visit.visit_id, Patient.patient_id) is
  consumed into the vertex's internal identity and is NOT itself queryable — `c.claim_id`
  silently returns null. Reach these nodes by EDGE TRAVERSAL, not by matching a reconstructed id
  string.
- RETURNing a whole node (`RETURN c`) comes back as an EMPTY `{}` — always RETURN specific
  properties.
- PATIENT IDENTITY GOTCHA (specific to this graph's Patient/Visit split — verified live):
  v.patient_mrn / v.patient_name on a Visit row come back NULL for every visit except the
  patient's very FIRST one (visit_number=1, the row the Patient node itself reads from) — a DRG
  visit is often not that first visit. Do NOT read patient identity off the Visit
  you're holding; traverse to Patient instead, which works from ANY of that patient's visits in
  either direction: `MATCH (v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(c:Claim {claim_number:$n}) MATCH
  (p:Patient)-[:HAS_VISIT]->(v) RETURN p.patient_mrn, p.patient_name` (verified live: returns
  the correct MRN/name even when v.patient_mrn itself is null).
- Claim's queryable human identifier is `claim_number` (e.g. 'MR_01'). Claim.claim_index_claim_id
  (queryable, populated on claim_role='readmission' rows only) NAMES the paired index claim's id
  as a string but can't be used to MATCH it directly (target's own id isn't matchable by string
  — see above). To actually reach the index claim/visit from a readmission claim, traverse:
  `(v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(rdm:Claim {claim_number:$rm})`, `(v)-[:REVISIT_OF]->(prevVisit:Visit)`,
  `(prevVisit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(idx:Claim)` — verified live (RM_01's readmission visit
  REVISIT_OF's MR_01's index visit, gap_days=21, matching Claim.claim_gap_days).
- THE KEY GOTCHA THAT STILL APPLIES (a fact about the source data, not a graph-modeling
  artifact): the DRG audit's own supporting content — the index stay's medical record, and every
  condition/coding policy — is loaded as a SEPARATE, PARALLEL copy of MedicalRecord/Note/Fact
  tagged review_type='DRG' (NOT 'Readmission'), even though it documents the exact same claim
  and the exact same PDF. `(Visit)-[:DOCUMENTED_BY]->(MedicalRecord)` DOES resolve correctly —
  just remember to filter `{review_type:'DRG'}` on the MedicalRecord, since the same Visit also
  has a review_type='Readmission' MedicalRecord pointing at the identical PDF content:
    MATCH (v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(c:Claim {claim_number:'MR_01'}),
          (v)-[:DOCUMENTED_BY]->(mr:MedicalRecord {review_type:'DRG'})-[:HAS_NOTE]->(n:Note)
- Code is a shared dimension across ALL review types and code systems (ICD-10-CM, ICD-10-PCS,
  APR-DRG, etc.) — filter by `code_system` too whenever a bare code could collide.
- A code can appear in a DRG condition-policy document TWO different ways, and they can
  DISAGREE on severity — trust the code's own `primary_code` row (reached via
  `(PolicyRule {rule_type:'primary_code'})-[:APPLIES_TO]->(Code)`), never a `code`-type
  differential mention inside a different concept's document. Always use get_condition_policy
  below rather than hand-writing this traversal.
- Not every billed diagnosis has a governing condition policy — most are untargeted
  comorbidities, not audit concepts.


Domain knowledge for this review type:

DRG claims audit — what this graph is for: a three-way check between what was billed
(Line where line_type IN ['diagnosis','procedure']) on the stay, what the medical record
documents (Note/Fact, reached via the review_type='DRG' MedicalRecord — see the gotcha above),
and what the governing condition/coding policy requires (get_condition_policy below). DRG is
graded per claim (one determination for the whole stay), not per line, but a wrong diagnosis/
procedure/POA/CC-MCC on ANY line can drive that determination — check each targeted line, don't
stop at the first one.

Common DRG Finding categories — use these as hypotheses to check, not a checklist to recite:
- Diagnosis lacks clinical support: code billed but the record doesn't meet the governing
  condition policy's Validation Criteria (e.g. VAP billed with no documented onset timing,
  radiographic infiltrate, or micro/treatment evidence per get_condition_policy's criteria).
  Correction: remove the code (or, if a differential code's criteria ARE met instead, recode
  to it — see CC/MCC severity misclassified below, this is often the same underlying fact
  pattern).
- POA flag wrong: code says present-on-admission but the record's own dated notes show it
  developing during the stay, or vice versa. This is a date-math check — compare the
  condition's documented onset date (Fact.printed_date / Note.note_date) against
  Claim.claim_admit_date — not a keyword search.
- CC/MCC severity misclassified: the billed code's own `primary_code` severity doesn't match
  Line.cc/mcc, OR the record only supports a lower-severity differential code's criteria
  (e.g. J18.9 [CC] documented, not the [MCC] J95.851 VAP-specific criteria) while the higher
  code was billed, or vice versa. Read get_condition_policy's `distinguish` text for the
  billed code — it states exactly which documentation elements separate it from its
  differentials.
- Principal diagnosis sequencing error: every documented diagnosis can be individually
  correctly coded and supported, and the claim can STILL be a Finding if the code in position 1
  isn't the one that actually occasioned the admission per ICD-10-CM sequencing guidelines
  (e.g. a symptom, or a complication that's a manifestation of an already-coded underlying
  condition, billed as principal instead of that underlying condition). Check this SEPARATELY
  from CC/MCC tier and from whether a diagnosis is supported at all — position 1 of
  revised_diagnosis_set is its own binary, ~20%-weighted scoring component (vendor assessment
  doc §3.1.e), distinct from the "Remaining Codes" presence-match component.
- Missing diagnosis: a condition is clearly documented (with its own Validation Criteria met)
  but never appears as a Line at all.
- Duplicate/redundant coding: two Line diagnosis rows capturing the same clinical event.
- Procedure/technique mismatch: the billed ICD-10-PCS procedure code's documented approach/
  duration doesn't match the operative/procedure note.
- Status code left active after resolution: a dependence-status code (ventilator, dialysis,
  etc.) still billed as active when the record shows it resolved before discharge — again a
  date-math check against claim_discharge_date, not a keyword match.
- Missing procedure code: a performed procedure (e.g. "Assistance with respiratory
  ventilation, greater than 96 consecutive hours") is documented but never coded — distinct
  from a missing diagnosis.

Patient/facility identifiers for a DRG claim are NOT on the Claim node itself, and NOT
reliably on its Visit node either (see SCHEMA's Patient identity gotcha) — traverse
`(Patient)-[:HAS_VISIT]->(Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(Claim)` to get them, or, for MR_01..MR_10 only,
look them up on the paired readmission claim.

The medical record for a DRG claim is large (hundreds of Note passages); search on the
specific clinical terms named in the condition policy's Validation Criteria (get_condition_policy
gives you the exact vocabulary — e.g. "endotracheal", "purulent", "PaO2/FiO2") rather than a
generic term.

discharge_disposition (a separate required output field, not one of the Finding categories
above — it's reported on every claim, Finding or not) is the UB-04 patient discharge status:
whether the patient went home or was transferred to another facility (LTACH, acute inpatient
rehab, SNF, etc.), which matters for post-acute-care-transfer payment policy. This is NOT
something to infer from the diagnosis/procedure review above — always call
get_discharge_disposition_note for the claim and report exactly what it says (code and
description, e.g. "63 - Discharged/transferred to LTACH"); null only if it returns no rows.


Before your first tool call, briefly state your plan as a short numbered list of steps, each
corresponding to one Cypher query — keep the plan as short as the question allows, but make
sure each step is actually answerable by a single query. Revise the plan if a result surprises
you (e.g. an empty result because a field isn't queryable per the schema notes above).

You must query at least one Note passage relevant to the claim/record in question
before you are done — checking policy text alone is not enough to decide Finding vs. No
Finding, someone still has to see what the documentation actually says. Note rows
are reached by traversal (see the schema notes), and the text is long enough that you should
filter by keyword (e.g. `WHERE toLower(e.text) CONTAINS toLower('meniscus')`) rather than
pulling every passage. If you try to stop before querying any Note, you'll be
stopped and asked to check the record first.

Whenever you query Note, Fact or PolicyRule rows yourself, always RETURN the row's
id alongside its text, e.g. `RETURN id(n) AS source_id, n.title AS title, n.text AS text`. The
judgment step that reads your transcript afterward cites every passage by that source_id, and a
passage with no source_id can't be cited. The skill tools already return it.

Cypher literal strings break on an unescaped apostrophe (e.g. `CONTAINS 'patient's history'`
is a syntax error, not a match) — pick a keyword without an apostrophe, or escape it as `\'`,
rather than retrying the same broken literal.

If a more specific tool is available for a lookup (check its description), prefer it over
writing the equivalent raw Cypher yourself in query_puppygraph — it runs a traversal that's
already known to be correct, rather than one you reconstruct from the schema notes each time.

Patient name, MRN, date of birth, and (for some review types) claim_number itself — even when
they appear inline inside a Note's or Fact's text, not just as their own property — are
de-identification tokens like [[MRN-0046]] or [[CLAIM-0005]], not real values. The double
brackets are literal characters of the value, not markdown or wiki-link markup to strip out —
verified live: passing a "cleaned up" claim_number with the brackets removed as a tool argument
silently matches zero rows (the underlying property is the bracketed token, not the bare text
inside it), which then looks like the record has no data at all. Copy a token byte-for-byte,
brackets included, everywhere it's used: as a tool call argument, in Cypher, and quoted verbatim
in a citation. Never remark on the token format, guess what real value it stands for, or treat
its presence as unusual — a separate step restores the real values afterward, outside anything
you do here.

Once you've gathered the claim line detail, the governing policy, and at least one relevant
medical-record passage, stop calling tools and reply with a short plain-text note of what you
found. Do NOT render a Finding/No Finding determination yourself — a separate step decides
that from what you retrieve here. Don't fabricate or guess at data you haven't queried.

Chief Complaint: "Level 1 trauma - ejected driver, MVC vs tree, unresponsive at scene."
Triage Acuity ESI 1 (resuscitation)
Arrival EMS, ground (Level 1 trauma activation)
Disposition Admit - ICU
History of Present Illness
[[NAME-0002]] is a 32-year-old woman without significant past medical history who was involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision
as the unrestrained driver of a passenger vehicle that struck a tree at an estimated 60 mph. The patient was ejected from the vehicle and
was found unresponsive at the scene. EMS assessment on arrival documented GCS 8 with tachycardia (HR 130) and hypotension (SBP
78). Two large-bore intravenous lines and 1L of crystalloid were administered en route. Level 1 trauma activation was called and the
patient was transported to our trauma bay. On arrival GCS had improved to 12 with continued hemodynamic instability. Focused
Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) was positive in multiple views, and CT trauma panscan demonstrated Grade IV splenic
laceration, Grade II liver laceration, pelvic ring injury with active extravasation, right femur fracture, and right hemopneumothorax with rib
fractures. Emergency intubation was performed for airway protection. Massive transfusion protocol was activated, and the patient was
transferred to the operating room for damage-control laparotomy with splenectomy, followed by IR embolization for pelvic bleeding.
Past Medical / Surgical History
[p.653] Medical: None significant per family. Surgical: None reported.

1 | Grade IV splenic laceration status post emergent splenectomy
2 | Open-book pelvic ring injury (Tile B1) with external fixator placement
3 | Right femoral shaft fracture status post intramedullary nailing
4 | Traumatic right hemopneumothorax status post tube thoracostomy
5 | Rib fractures (right 4-8) with flail chest physiology
6 | Grade II liver laceration - non-operative management
7 | Rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury (KDIGO 2), non-dialysis-requiring
8 | Post-hemorrhagic anemia requiring transfusion (8 units PRBC total)
9 | Acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation

11 | Traumatic brain injury (mild - GCS 12 initial, resolved)
12 | Catheter-associated deep vein thrombosis (right femoral)

15 | Post-traumatic stress reaction
Social / Family History
Lives independently; employed; family reports occasional alcohol use, no illicit drug use, non-smoker. Family history unremarkable.
Review of Systems
Limited by acute presentation; unresponsive at scene; polytrauma with multi-system involvement.

Vitals: 35.9 degC | HR 130 | BP 78/44 (MAP 55) | RR 22 | SpO2 92% NRB. General: young adult in extremis with obvious multi-system
trauma. HEENT: pupils equal and reactive; multiple scalp abrasions and hematoma; midface stable. Cardiac: tachycardic, regular.
Respiratory: decreased breath sounds right, chest wall crepitus and paradoxical movement (flail). Abdomen: distended, tender, seatbelt
sign. Pelvis: unstable to lateral compression; pelvic binder applied. Extremities: obvious right thigh deformity with shortening and
external rotation; distal pulses palpable. Neuro: GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5) improved from 8 in the field; no focal deficits.

WBC 24.5; Hgb 6.8 (initial); platelets 145; PT 16.2, INR 1.5; fibrinogen 145 (low); Na 138, K 4.2, Cl 100, CO2 18, BUN 22, creatinine 1.3;

PaCO2 32 / PaO2 88 on NRB.
Imaging (Pertinent)

intervention. Chest Radiograph, Portable AP: Chest tube in good position; improved pneumothorax. See the Diagnostic Imaging
section for the full report.
Assessment
32-year-old woman previously healthy presenting with severe polytrauma from high-speed MVC including Grade IV splenic laceration
with hemorrhagic shock, pelvic ring injury with active extravasation, right femur fracture, right hemopneumothorax with flail chest, and
Grade II liver laceration. High illness severity requiring damage-control resuscitation and staged trauma surgery.
Plan
1. Hemorrhagic shock: massive transfusion protocol; damage-control laparotomy with splenectomy; IR embolization for pelvic bleeding;
resuscitation to endpoints.
2. Pelvic ring injury: pelvic binder; external fixation when hemodynamically stable.
3. Femur fracture: skeletal traction; intramedullary nailing when stable.
4. Hemopneumothorax: chest tube placed; monitor output and lung expansion.
5. Respiratory failure: mechanical ventilation; lung-protective settings.
6. Coagulopathy: TXA; FFP and platelets per MTP.
7. Antimicrobials: pre-op cefazolin.
8. VTE prophylaxis: mechanical only until hemostasis; convert to pharmacologic when stable.

Admit: TSICU. Condition: critical.
Vitals: continuous telemetry, arterial-line BP, SpO2, ICP if indicated; hourly assessment; strict I/O.

Admit: 2026-02-08 Transfer: 2026-05-23
LOS: 103 days
Reason for Admission: Severe polytrauma with hemorrhagic shock following motor vehicle collision.
Admission Diagnoses
Multi-system trauma with hemorrhagic shock following MVC
Discharge / Transfer Diagnoses
Resolving polytrauma from MVC; status post splenectomy; status post pelvic external fixation; status post right femoral intramedullary
nailing; resolved right hemopneumothorax; resolved MSSA VAP; right femoral DVT on anticoagulation; resolved rhabdomyolysis and

Hospital Course
[[NAME-0002]] presented as a Level 1 trauma activation following a high-speed motor vehicle collision with ejection resulting in severe
polytrauma with hemorrhagic shock. Emergency damage-control laparotomy with splenectomy was performed, followed by IR
embolization of a bleeding right internal iliac branch. The course was complicated by right hemopneumothorax requiring tube
thoracostomy, pelvic ring injury requiring external fixation on ICU day 3, right femoral shaft fracture requiring intramedullary nailing on ICU
day 4, Grade II liver laceration managed non-operatively, rhabdomyolysis with AKI managed with aggressive hydration, hospital-acquired
methicillin-susceptible S. aureus ventilator-associated pneumonia treated with cefazolin, catheter-associated right common femoral DVT
treated with therapeutic anticoagulation, post-traumatic stress reaction managed with supportive care and psychiatric consultation, and
profound ICU-acquired weakness. Post-splenectomy pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenzae vaccines were
administered. Extubation was successful on ICU day 9 with brief VAP requiring aggressive pulmonary toileting rather than reintubation.
The patient is transferred to an acute inpatient rehabilitation facility for continued orthopedic and functional recovery with
non-weight-bearing precautions on the right lower extremity.

Vitals: Tmax 37.2 degC | HR 79 | MAP 76 | RR 15 | SpO2 96%. Airway/Support: room air, ambulatory oxygenation preserved. General:
Alert, interactive, comfortable; participating in therapy. HEENT: mucous membranes moist, no scleral icterus. Cardiac: Regular rate and
rhythm; no murmur; well perfused. Respiratory: Clear to diminished; good air movement; tolerating trach collar. Abdomen: soft,
non-distended, +bowel sounds; PEG site clean and dry. Extremities: pulses intact. Neuro: Alert and oriented; CAM-ICU negative;
strength improving with rehab. Skin/Lines: Skin intact; healing well; ambulating with assistance. Extremities: ex-fix in place; healing
incisions; non-weight-bearing right leg.

CBC: WBC 7.8 x103/uL, Hgb 10.4 g/dL, Hct 31%, platelets 225 x109/L (neutrophils 74%). BMP: Na 138, K 4.3, Cl 102, CO2 25, BUN 22,
creatinine 1.10 mg/dL, glucose 155 mg/dL, Ca 8.6, Mg 2.0, Phos 3.8. ABG (07:00): pH 7.40 / PaCO2 38 / PaO2 86 / HCO3 24; lactate
1.4 mmol/L; P/F ratio 298.
Imaging (Pertinent)
No new imaging obtained today. Most recent radiograph reviewed and compared; findings consistent with the documented clinical
trajectory.
Condition & Functional Status at Transfer
Alert, oriented, and interactive. Room air with adequate oxygenation. Ambulating with walker and non-weight-bearing precautions on right
lower extremity. Tolerating oral diet with good intake. Hemodynamically stable. Pelvic external fixator in place. Multiple healing incisions.

1. Continue acute inpatient rehabilitation with intensive PT/OT.
2. Trauma Surgery follow-up in 2-4 weeks.
3. Orthopedic Surgery follow-up at 2 weeks for hardware assessment; non-weight-bearing precautions on right lower extremity for 6
weeks minimum.

8. Post-splenectomy precautions: emergency antibiotics for febrile illness, annual vaccinations, medical alert bracelet.
9. Return precautions: fever, respiratory decompensation, worsening leg swelling, bleeding, hardware pain or drainage.

Purpose Raises blood pressure when the body is in shock.
Dose & Route Titrated via IV infusion to maintain blood pressure.
Side Effects Decreased blood flow to hands/feet; irregular heartbeat.
Monitoring Continuous blood pressure and heart rate monitoring.
Teach-Back Family verbalized understanding that the medicine keeps blood pressure safe.
Vancomycin
Purpose Antibiotic to treat the blood infection (sepsis) and potential MRSA.
Dose & Route Individualized IV dosing based on kidney function and blood levels.
Side Effects Kidney injury (monitored daily); rash if given too fast (Red Man Syndrome).
Monitoring Daily labs; infuse slowly over at least 60 minutes.
Teach-Back Family able to state purpose; instructed to report rash or skin flushing.
Piperacillin-tazobactam (Zosyn)
Purpose Broad-spectrum antibiotic targeting pneumonia and gram-negative bacteria.
Dose & Route 4.5 g IV every 6 hours, extended infusion over 3 hours.
Side Effects Diarrhea; low potassium; allergic reaction (report rash immediately).
Monitoring Renal function, electrolytes daily.
Teach-Back Teach-back deferred - patient sedated. Education provided to son.
Pantoprazole (Protonix)
Purpose Protects the stomach lining while on stress-ulcer prophylaxis.
Dose & Route 40 mg IV once daily, transitioning to oral when tolerating feeds.
Side Effects Low magnesium with long-term use (monitored); headache.
Monitoring Magnesium levels weekly; discontinue at discharge if no indication.
Teach-Back Patient verbalized that medication protects the stomach.
Enoxaparin (Lovenox)
Purpose Blood thinner to prevent blood clots (DVT) in legs and lungs.
Dose & Route Prophylactic dose; adjusted if active clot is confirmed.
Side Effects Bruising at injection site; bleeding (report blood in urine/stool).
[p.49] Monitoring Daily CBC; watch for signs of bleeding.
Teach-Back Son acknowledged understanding of clot-prevention purpose and verbalized when to call
for help (unusual bleeding).
Insulin infusion / Sliding scale
Purpose Controls blood sugar (glucose) which rises during critical illness.
Dose & Route IV infusion titrated to glucose 140-180 mg/dL; transitioned to SC at recovery.
Side Effects
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): sweating, confusion, shakiness.
Monitoring Point-of-care glucose every 1-2 hours while on infusion.
Teach-Back Patient able to describe symptoms of low blood sugar at discharge planning.
Amiodarone
Purpose Corrects and prevents rapid irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation).
Dose & Route IV load then oral maintenance; dose adjusted per response.
Side Effects Thyroid problems, lung toxicity, liver effects (all monitored). Sensitivity to sunlight - use
sunscreen.
Monitoring Thyroid/liver labs monthly; chest X-ray annually; QT interval on ECG.
Teach-Back Family verbalized that patient needs ongoing monitoring after discharge. Written materials
provided.
Apixaban (Eliquis) - at discharge
Purpose Blood thinner for catheter-associated DVT (blood clot in neck vein).
Dose & Route 10 mg twice daily x 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily x at least 3 months.
Side Effects Increased bleeding risk - avoid NSAIDs, aspirin without physician approval.
Monitoring No routine lab monitoring required, but report unusual bleeding.
Teach-Back Patient and son demonstrated understanding of dose schedule and verbalized to avoid
ibuprofen. Written instruction sheet given.

### Findings from the Audit of DRG Claim MR_04

#### Claim and Patient Information
- **Patient MRN**: [[MRN-0002]]
- **Patient Name**: [[NAME-0002]]
- **Claim Number**: MR_04
- **Length of Stay**: 103 days (admitted on 2026-02-08 and transferred on 2026-05-23)
- **Discharge Disposition**: Transferred to an acute inpatient rehabilitation facility for ongoing recovery.

#### Billed Diagnoses with Relevant Findings
1. **S36.032A** — Major laceration of spleen, initial encounter [POA=Y, MCC]
   - **Policy Confirmation**: Supports MCC status with criteria including explicit identification of traumatic splenic injury.
   - **Clinical Support**: Documented as Grade IV splenic laceration, consistent with the MCC designation as confirmed by imaging and clinical notes.

2. **S72.302A** — Unspecified fracture of shaft of left femur, initial encounter for closed fracture [POA=Y, MCC]
   - **Policy Confirmation**: No specific governing policy was found targeting this code as a clinical priority for the audit.
   - **Clinical Note**: Billed description conflicts with the discharge summary; confirm with clinical notes.

3. **S27.4XXA** — Traumatic pneumothorax, initial encounter [POA=Y, MCC]
   - **Policy Confirmation**: Lacks a specific primary code policy but documented as a critical finding post-surgery.

4. **R57.01** — Cardiogenic shock [POA=Y, MCC]
   - **Policy Confirmation**: No specific governing policy was located for this code.

5. **J95.851** — Ventilator associated pneumonia [POA=Y, CC]
   - **Policy Confirmation**: The documentation supports MCC classification, with validation criteria requiring specific clinical signs and timing following intubation.

#### Billed Procedures of Interest
1. **Resection of spleen** — This procedure aligns with the principal diagnosis and is substantiated by clinical documentation.
2. **Insertion of endotracheal airway** and **Assistance with respiratory ventilation** — Both documented within the context of the ICU stay, focusing on the critical managed airway.

#### Relevant Medical Records Notes
1. **History & Physical (Admitting)**: Provides an overview of the trauma, injuries sustained, and critical interventions performed, confirming the severity of the injuries.
2. **Discharge/Transfer Summary**: Creates a complete picture of the initial conditions and management throughout the stay, emphasizing challenges such as VAP and the resolution of acute kidney injury.
3. **Infectious Diseases Consultation**: Highlights the development of ventilator-associated pneumonia shortly after intubation, necessitating continued antibiotic therapy.

### Summary of Findings
- **Diagnosis Support**: Most diagnoses, particularly S36.032A and J95.851, have robust clinical support documented throughout the hospitalization. 
- **Principal Diagnosis**: The principal diagnosis did not change; it remains classified as MCC supported by clinical documentation and imaging.
- **Discrepancies**: Some billed lines are found to conflict with the documentation provided, notably **S72.302A** which needs further confirmation due to varying clinical details across notes.

### Recommendations for Corrected Diagnosis and Procedures
- **Corrected List**:
  - Principal Diagnosis: S36.032A (Major laceration of spleen)
  - Additional Diagnoses: J95.851 (Ventilator associated pneumonia), S72.302A (if confirmed)
- **Procedures**: Confirm all procedures performed match documentation; any discrepancies need addressing with clinical staff.

This audit recommends meticulous review of the identified discrepancies before finalizing the coding and claims submission to ensure compliance and adequate reimbursement.

judge_messages.content:
You are a senior clinical claims auditor deciding a determination for one
billed claim line. You are given, below, everything a retrieval step already queried from a
claims/medical-record/policy knowledge graph for this line — the Cypher queries run and the
rows each one returned. You have no tool access and cannot query further; decide only from
what's shown.

Domain knowledge for this review type:

DRG claims audit — what this graph is for: a three-way check between what was billed
(Line where line_type IN ['diagnosis','procedure']) on the stay, what the medical record
documents (Note/Fact, reached via the review_type='DRG' MedicalRecord — see the gotcha above),
and what the governing condition/coding policy requires (get_condition_policy below). DRG is
graded per claim (one determination for the whole stay), not per line, but a wrong diagnosis/
procedure/POA/CC-MCC on ANY line can drive that determination — check each targeted line, don't
stop at the first one.

Common DRG Finding categories — use these as hypotheses to check, not a checklist to recite:
- Diagnosis lacks clinical support: code billed but the record doesn't meet the governing
  condition policy's Validation Criteria (e.g. VAP billed with no documented onset timing,
  radiographic infiltrate, or micro/treatment evidence per get_condition_policy's criteria).
  Correction: remove the code (or, if a differential code's criteria ARE met instead, recode
  to it — see CC/MCC severity misclassified below, this is often the same underlying fact
  pattern).
- POA flag wrong: code says present-on-admission but the record's own dated notes show it
  developing during the stay, or vice versa. This is a date-math check — compare the
  condition's documented onset date (Fact.printed_date / Note.note_date) against
  Claim.claim_admit_date — not a keyword search.
- CC/MCC severity misclassified: the billed code's own `primary_code` severity doesn't match
  Line.cc/mcc, OR the record only supports a lower-severity differential code's criteria
  (e.g. J18.9 [CC] documented, not the [MCC] J95.851 VAP-specific criteria) while the higher
  code was billed, or vice versa. Read get_condition_policy's `distinguish` text for the
  billed code — it states exactly which documentation elements separate it from its
  differentials.
- Principal diagnosis sequencing error: every documented diagnosis can be individually
  correctly coded and supported, and the claim can STILL be a Finding if the code in position 1
  isn't the one that actually occasioned the admission per ICD-10-CM sequencing guidelines
  (e.g. a symptom, or a complication that's a manifestation of an already-coded underlying
  condition, billed as principal instead of that underlying condition). Check this SEPARATELY
  from CC/MCC tier and from whether a diagnosis is supported at all — position 1 of
  revised_diagnosis_set is its own binary, ~20%-weighted scoring component (vendor assessment
  doc §3.1.e), distinct from the "Remaining Codes" presence-match component.
- Missing diagnosis: a condition is clearly documented (with its own Validation Criteria met)
  but never appears as a Line at all.
- Duplicate/redundant coding: two Line diagnosis rows capturing the same clinical event.
- Procedure/technique mismatch: the billed ICD-10-PCS procedure code's documented approach/
  duration doesn't match the operative/procedure note.
- Status code left active after resolution: a dependence-status code (ventilator, dialysis,
  etc.) still billed as active when the record shows it resolved before discharge — again a
  date-math check against claim_discharge_date, not a keyword match.
- Missing procedure code: a performed procedure (e.g. "Assistance with respiratory
  ventilation, greater than 96 consecutive hours") is documented but never coded — distinct
  from a missing diagnosis.

Patient/facility identifiers for a DRG claim are NOT on the Claim node itself, and NOT
reliably on its Visit node either (see SCHEMA's Patient identity gotcha) — traverse
`(Patient)-[:HAS_VISIT]->(Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(Claim)` to get them, or, for MR_01..MR_10 only,
look them up on the paired readmission claim.

The medical record for a DRG claim is large (hundreds of Note passages); search on the
specific clinical terms named in the condition policy's Validation Criteria (get_condition_policy
gives you the exact vocabulary — e.g. "endotracheal", "purulent", "PaO2/FiO2") rather than a
generic term.

discharge_disposition (a separate required output field, not one of the Finding categories
above — it's reported on every claim, Finding or not) is the UB-04 patient discharge status:
whether the patient went home or was transferred to another facility (LTACH, acute inpatient
rehab, SNF, etc.), which matters for post-acute-care-transfer payment policy. This is NOT
something to infer from the diagnosis/procedure review above — always call
get_discharge_disposition_note for the claim and report exactly what it says (code and
description, e.g. "63 - Discharged/transferred to LTACH"); null only if it returns no rows.


Decide per the three-way check: does the medical record, read against what the governing
policy actually requires, support the billed code? Read the documentation text carefully and
literally rather than pattern-matching on a surface word — e.g. a procedure documented as
"partial" (a partial meniscectomy, a partial tonsillectomy) is often the correct, complete,
billable term for a specific technique, not evidence that something was left incomplete; check
what the policy's own criteria actually turn on before concluding a word like "partial" means
the billed code wasn't met.

Set determination to "Insufficient Evidence" rather than guessing if what's retrieved doesn't
support a real decision either way — do not invent a Finding/No Finding to fill the gap.

system_note is the auditor note a human reviewer reads on EVERY claim, Finding or not — write
it with explicit citations (document/section/page) and reasoning a reviewer could audit line by
line; a correct determination with a
vague, citation-free note still scores as a weak note (see the quality bar in the schema
field's own description).

rationale_letter is a SEPARATE, formal appeal-ready letter to the provider — only written when
determination is Finding (null otherwise). It restates the finding and its basis for an
external, non-technical reader, not a repeat of system_note's internal auditor reasoning.

Page numbers: a medical-record note can span several PDF pages, and its page_start/page_end
are not the page of any particular line in it. In a long note's text, a [p.N] marker means the
text after it (up to the next marker) is on physical page N; cite that page in system_note,
never a note's page_start/page_end range. A note whose page_start equals its page_end is all on
that page. In a multi-page note with no marker before the line, name the note without a page.

evidence_cited must reference only passages that actually appear in the retrieved rows above.
Each entry is the source_id of the one row the quote comes from, copied exactly, and the quote
copied verbatim from that row's text, character for character: don't wrap part of it in
quotation marks, fix a typo, or drop a word or code from the middle. Never invent or recall one. Code checks each quote
against that row and fills in the document, section and page from it, so a quote that isn't in
the cited row, or a source_id that wasn't retrieved, is dropped. Each quote is ONE contiguous
passage from a single row: if you need two separate passages, give two separate evidence_cited
entries rather than joining them with "..."; a stitched-together quote can't be verified. Rows
with no source_id (claim lines, code descriptions, a tool's own summary rows) aren't citable;
cite the record or policy row behind them instead.

Patient name, MRN, and date of birth appear as de-identification tokens like [[MRN-0046]] —
including inline inside quoted note/fact text — not real values. Reproduce them exactly as
given in system_note, rationale_letter, and evidence_cited quotes; a separate step restores
the real values afterward. Never remark on the token format or guess/reconstruct what it stands
for.

discharge_disposition, finding_reason, recovery_type, skilled_services,
adjusted_date_of_service, corrected_revenue_code, adjusted_units_billed,
revised_diagnosis_set, and revised_procedure_set are only meaningful for specific review types
(DRG, Readmission, SNF, SNF, SNF, SNF, DRG, and DRG respectively) — see each field's own schema
description and this review type's domain notes above to know whether to populate it; leave it
null when this review type doesn't call for it.

If this is a DRG review: you are deciding for the WHOLE claim in one pass, not one line — check
every diagnosis and procedure line given to you (POA, CC/MCC tier, whether it's still
supported), not just the one the question happens to name first. revised_diagnosis_set and
revised_procedure_set must each be the claim's COMPLETE corrected list (every code that should
remain billed, in the same shape as what you were given, position 1 = principal diagnosis) —
not a delta of only the line(s) that changed. code_decisions is what's scored: one entry per
billed code, each exactly once, plus additions, with the POA and CC/MCC tier each diagnosis
should carry, and the evidence_cited IDs behind every change. Code checks it and builds the
corrected lists from it.

Question: Audit DRG claim MR_04's full coding for this admission — this is ONE determination for the whole stay, not per code, but check every line below (not just the first) since any one of them can drive the claim-level determination.
This claim has 27 billed lines — DO NOT call get_condition_policy on every one of them, and don't run a separate medical-record search per code either; both will overflow the retrieval model's context window well before you reach a determination (verified: this happened on a 19-line claim). Triage first: look for the principal diagnosis, any CC/MCC-tier code, and any code whose severity/support looks contestable from the billed description alone, and spend your policy/note lookups on THOSE — a routine, clearly-supported comorbidity (e.g. well-documented chronic hypertension or diabetes with no CC/MCC flag) doesn't need its own policy lookup. Batch related terms into one keyword search where you can rather than one search per condition.

  1. 0BH17EZ — Insertion of endotracheal airway into trachea, via natural or artificial opening

Does the documentation and each code's governing condition policy support it as coded — including POA status, CC/MCC severity tier, and principal-diagnosis sequencing (position 1)? If this is a Finding, give the claim's COMPLETE corrected diagnosis list (position 1 = principal) and COMPLETE corrected procedure list — not just the code(s) that changed — plus the discharge disposition documented in the record.

Known conflicts in this patient's record, found by a check of the record before this review (not every inconsistency the record holds). Each names the side not to rely on, where the patient's own documentation shows which side is right:
- section_not_this_patient / not_documentation: the whole section describes another patient, or is a billing summary or a query to the physician. It is not evidence: don't cite it or rely on it.
- do not trust: record_line: don't rely on the quoted line (the rest of its note stands); rely on the basis instead.
- do not trust: billed_line: the patient's own documentation contradicts this billed line. Check it as a likely correction, citing the basis.
- do not trust: either: the record doesn't settle it; read both sides. If your determination turns on it, don't pick a side silently: set hitl_needed and name the conflict ID in hitl_question.

Cardiac: tachycardic, regular.\nRespiratory: decreased breath sounds right, chest wall crepitus and paradoxical movement (flail). Abdomen: distended, tender, seatbelt\nsign. Pelvis: unstable to lateral compression; pelvic binder applied. Extremities: obvious right thigh deformity with shortening and\nexternal rotation; distal pulses palpable. Neuro: GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5) improved from 8 in the field; no focal deficits.\nLaboratory Data\nWBC 24.5; Hgb 6.8 (initial); platelets 145; PT 16.2, INR 1.5; fibrinogen 145 (low); Na 138, K 4.2, Cl 100, CO2 18, BUN 22, creatinine 1.3;\nglucose 178; lactate 5.4 mmol/L; ethanol negative; drug screen negative; troponin negative. ABG pH 7.24 /\nPaCO2 32 / PaO2 88 on NRB.\nImaging (Pertinent)\n[p.757] CT Trauma Panscan: Multi-system trauma with hemodynamically significant splenic and pelvic hemorrhage requiring immediate\nintervention. See the Diagnostic Imaging\nsection for the full report.\nAssessment\n32-year-old woman previously healthy presenting with severe polytrauma from high-speed MVC including Grade IV splenic laceration\nwith hemorrhagic shock, pelvic ring injury with active extravasation, right femur fracture, right hemopneumothorax with flail chest, and\nGrade II liver laceration. High illness severity requiring damage-control resuscitation and staged trauma surgery.\nPlan\n1. Hemorrhagic shock: massive transfusion protocol; damage-control laparotomy with splenectomy; IR embolization for pelvic bleeding;\nresuscitation to endpoints.\n2. Pelvic ring injury: pelvic binder; external fixation when hemodynamically stable.\n3. Femur fracture: skeletal traction; intramedullary nailing when stable.\n4. Hemopneumothorax: chest tube placed; monitor output and lung expansion.\n5. Respiratory failure: mechanical ventilation; lung-protective settings.\n6. Coagulopathy: TXA; FFP and platelets per MTP.\n7. Antimicrobials: pre-op cefazolin.\n8. VTE prophylaxis: mechanical only until hemostasis; convert to pharmacologic when stable.\nElectronically signed: Thomas Kowalski, MD, Surgical Critical Care   |   2026-02-08 16:00\nAdmission Orders\nAdmit: TSICU. Condition: critical.\nVitals: continuous telemetry, arterial-line BP, SpO2, ICP if indicated; hourly assessment; strict I/O.\nVentilation: lung-protective; low tidal volume 6 mL/kg IBW; monitor for ARDS.\nHemodynamics: norepinephrine to MAP >= 65; damage-control resuscitation; MTP activation as needed; monitor thromboelastography.\nOrthopedics: maintain pelvic binder pre-fixator; skeletal traction for right lower extremity; neurovascular checks q1h.\nAntithrombotics: hold pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis until hemostasis established then initiate low molecular weight heparin at 48\nhours if stable.\nAntimicrobials: cefazolin 2 g pre-op prophylaxis; escalate as indicated.\nLabs: serial CBC/CMP/CK/lactate q4h; ABG q6h; coags initially, then daily.\nProphylaxis: pantoprazole 40 mg IV daily; SCDs; glycemic control 140-180."}, {"source_id": "NOTE-Medical-Records-1-15-MR_04.pdf-n903", "title": "Discharge / Transfer Summary", "note_type": "Discharge / Transfer Summary", "section_path": "Transfer / Discharge Summary", "note_date": null, "page_start": 838, "page_end": 839, "text": "Discharge / Transfer Summary\n[p.838] Attending: Dr. Thomas Kowalski, MD (Critical Care Medicine)\nAdmit: 2026-02-08 Transfer: 2026-05-23\nLOS: 103 days\nReason for Admission: Severe polytrauma with hemorrhagic shock following motor vehicle collision.\nAdmission Diagnoses\nMulti-system trauma with hemorrhagic shock following MVC\nDischarge / Transfer Diagnoses\nResolving polytrauma from MVC; status post splenectomy; status post pelvic external fixation; status post right femoral intramedullary\nnailing; resolved right hemopneumothorax; resolved MSSA VAP; right femoral DVT on anticoagulation; resolved rhabdomyolysis and\nAKI; post-splenectomy immunocompromise; ICU-acquired weakness; post-traumatic stress reaction.\nHospital Course\n[[NAME-0002]] presented as a Level 1 trauma activation following a high-speed motor vehicle collision with ejection resulting in severe\npolytrauma with hemorrhagic shock. Emergency damage-control laparotomy with splenectomy was performed, followed by IR\nembolization of a bleeding right internal iliac branch. The course was complicated by right hemopneumothorax requiring tube\nthoracostomy, pelvic ring injury requiring external fixation on ICU day 3, right femoral shaft fracture requiring intramedullary nailing on ICU\nday 4, Grade II liver laceration managed non-operatively, rhabdomyolysis with AKI managed with aggressive hydration, hospital-acquired\nmethicillin-susceptible S. aureus ventilator-associated pneumonia treated with cefazolin, catheter-associated right common femoral DVT\ntreated with therapeutic anticoagulation, post-traumatic stress reaction managed with supportive care and psychiatric consultation, and\nprofound ICU-acquired weakness. Post-splenectomy pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenzae vaccines were\nadministered. Extubation was successful on ICU day 9 with brief VAP requiring aggressive pulmonary toileting rather than reintubation.\nThe patient is transferred to an acute inpatient rehabilitation facility for continued orthopedic and functional recovery with\nnon-weight-bearing precautions on the right lower extremity.\nPhysical Examination\nVitals: Tmax 37.2 degC | HR 79 | MAP 76 | RR 15 | SpO2 96%. Airway/Support: room air, ambulatory oxygenation preserved. General:\nAlert, interactive, comfortable; participating in therapy. HEENT: mucous membranes moist, no scleral icterus. Cardiac: Regular rate and\nrhythm; no murmur; well perfused. Respiratory: Clear to diminished; good air movement; tolerating trach collar. Abdomen: soft,\nnon-distended, +bowel sounds; PEG site clean and dry. Extremities: pulses intact. Neuro: Alert and oriented; CAM-ICU negative;\nstrength improving with rehab. Skin/Lines: Skin intact; healing well; ambulating with assistance. Extremities: ex-fix in place; healing\nincisions; non-weight-bearing right leg.\nLaboratory Data (Pertinent)\nCBC: WBC 7.8 x103/uL, Hgb 10.4 g/dL, Hct 31%, platelets 225 x109/L (neutrophils 74%). BMP: Na 138, K 4.3, Cl 102, CO2 25, BUN 22,\ncreatinine 1.10 mg/dL, glucose 155 mg/dL, Ca 8.6, Mg 2.0, Phos 3.8. ABG (07:00): pH 7.40 / PaCO2 38 / PaO2 86 / HCO3 24; lactate\n1.4 mmol/L; P/F ratio 298.\nImaging (Pertinent)\nNo new imaging obtained today. Most recent radiograph reviewed and compared; findings consistent with the documented clinical\ntrajectory.\nCondition & Functional Status at Transfer\nAlert, oriented, and interactive. Room air with adequate oxygenation. Ambulating with walker and non-weight-bearing precautions on right\nlower extremity. Tolerating oral diet with good intake. Hemodynamically stable. Pelvic external fixator in place. Multiple healing incisions.\nTransfer Medications\nMedication | Dose | Route | Frequency | Indication\n[p.839] Cefazolin | 2 g | IV | q8h (finish course) | MSSA VAP\nApixaban | 5 mg | PO | BID | Right femoral DVT\nSertraline | 25 mg | PO | Daily | Post-traumatic stress\nAcetaminophen | 1000 mg | PO | q6h scheduled | Pain control\nOxycodone | 5-10 mg | PO | q4h PRN | Breakthrough pain\nGabapentin | 300 mg | PO | TID | Neuropathic pain\nPantoprazole | 40 mg | PO | Daily | Stress ulcer prophylaxis\nDocusate | 100 mg | PO | BID | Constipation prophylaxis\nMultivitamin | 1 tab | PO | Daily | Recovery\nFollow-Up & Recommendations\n1. Continue acute inpatient rehabilitation with intensive PT/OT.\n2. Trauma Surgery follow-up in 2-4 weeks.\n3. Orthopedic Surgery follow-up at 2 weeks for hardware assessment; non-weight-bearing precautions on right lower extremity for 6\nweeks minimum.\n4. Complete MSSA VAP antibiotic course.\n5. Continue anticoagulation for DVT; hematology follow-up.\n6. Primary care follow-up for overall recovery.\n7. Psychiatry follow-up for post-traumatic stress.\n8. Post-splenectomy precautions: emergency antibiotics for febrile illness, annual vaccinations, medical alert bracelet.\n9. Teach-back is documented\nfor each session. Learning barriers: critical illness and delirium early in the course; participation improved with recovery. Interpreter not\nrequired (English).\nNorepinephrine (Levophed)\nPurpose Raises blood pressure when the body is in shock.\nDose & Route Titrated via IV infusion to maintain blood pressure.\nSide Effects Decreased blood flow to hands/feet; irregular heartbeat.\nMonitoring Continuous blood pressure and heart rate monitoring.\nTeach-Back Family verbalized understanding that the medicine keeps blood pressure safe.\nVancomycin\nPurpose Antibiotic to treat the blood infection (sepsis) and potential MRSA.\nDose & Route Individualized IV dosing based on kidney function and blood levels.\nSide Effects Kidney injury (monitored daily); rash if given too fast (Red Man Syndrome).\nMonitoring Daily labs; infuse slowly over at least 60 minutes.\nTeach-Back Family able to state purpose; instructed to report rash or skin flushing.\nPiperacillin-tazobactam (Zosyn)\nPurpose Broad-spectrum antibiotic targeting pneumonia and gram-negative bacteria.\nDose & Route 4.5 g IV every 6 hours, extended infusion over 3 hours.\nSide Effects Diarrhea; low potassium; allergic reaction (report rash immediately).\nMonitoring Renal function, electrolytes daily.\nTeach-Back Teach-back deferred - patient sedated. Education provided to son.\nPantoprazole (Protonix)\nPurpose Protects the stomach lining while on stress-ulcer prophylaxis.\nDose & Route 40 mg IV once daily, transitioning to oral when tolerating feeds.\nSide Effects Low magnesium with long-term use (monitored); headache.\nMonitoring Magnesium levels weekly; discontinue at discharge if no indication.\nTeach-Back Patient verbalized that medication protects the stomach.\nEnoxaparin (Lovenox)\nPurpose Blood thinner to prevent blood clots (DVT) in legs and lungs.\nDose & Route Prophylactic dose; adjusted if active clot is confirmed.\nSide Effects Bruising at injection site; bleeding (report blood in urine/stool).\n[p.49] Monitoring Daily CBC; watch for signs of bleeding.\nTeach-Back Son acknowledged understanding of clot-prevention purpose and verbalized when to call\nfor help (unusual bleeding).\nInsulin infusion / Sliding scale\nPurpose Controls blood sugar (glucose) which rises during critical illness.\nDose & Route IV infusion titrated to glucose 140-180 mg/dL; transitioned to SC at recovery.\nSide Effects\nLow blood sugar (hypoglycemia): sweating, confusion, shakiness.\nMonitoring Point-of-care glucose every 1-2 hours while on infusion.\nTeach-Back Patient able to describe symptoms of low blood sugar at discharge planning.\nAmiodarone\nPurpose Corrects and prevents rapid irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation).\nDose & Route IV load then oral maintenance; dose adjusted per response.\nSide Effects Thyroid problems, lung toxicity, liver effects (all monitored). Sensitivity to sunlight - use\nsunscreen.\nMonitoring Thyroid/liver labs monthly; chest X-ray annually; QT interval on ECG.\nTeach-Back Family verbalized that patient needs ongoing monitoring after discharge. Written materials\nprovided.\nApixaban (Eliquis) - at discharge\nPurpose Blood thinner for catheter-associated DVT (blood clot in neck vein).\nDose & Route 10 mg twice daily x 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily x at least 3 months.\nSide Effects Increased bleeding risk - avoid NSAIDs, aspirin without physician approval.\nMonitoring No routine lab monitoring required, but report unusual bleeding.\nTeach-Back Patient and son demonstrated understanding of dose schedule and verbalized to avoid\nibuprofen. Written instruction sheet given.\nEducation Log Summary (All Topics)\nDate | Topic | Learner | Content Taught | Evaluation\n02/08 | Trauma diagnosis and ICU\ncare | Family | Explained the injuries, surgeries required, and the ICU\nenvironment. | Family verbalized\nunderstanding of the\nseverity.\n02/10 | Damage-control surgery\nand staged procedures | Family | Reviewed the concept of staged trauma surgery with initial\ncontrol followed by definitive repair. | Family verbalized\nunderstanding.\n02/14 | Extubation and\npost-operative recovery | Patient/Family | Reviewed the extubation process and pulmonary care after\nsurgery. | Patient/family\nverbalized\nunderstanding.\n02/19 | Weight-bearing precautions\nand mobility | Patient/Family | Reviewed non-weight-bearing precautions for right lower\nextremity and safe transfer techniques. | Return demonstration\ncorrect with cues.\n02/21 | DVT and anticoagulation | Patient/Family | Explained the leg clot, reason for anticoagulation, and bleeding\nprecautions. | Patient/family\nverbalized\nunderstanding.\n02/23 | Post-splenectomy\nprecautions and\nvaccinations | Patient/Family | Reviewed importance of vaccinations, infection precautions,\nand when to seek care. | Return demonstration\ncorrect.\nDate | Topic | Learner | Content Taught | Evaluation\n[p.835] 02/24 | Post-traumatic stress and\npsychological recovery | Patient/Family | Discussed common post-traumatic stress symptoms and\ncoping strategies. | Patient/family\nengaged.\n03/01 | Discharge medications and\nfollow-up | Patient/Family | Reconciled discharge medication list and reviewed follow-up\nappointments. | Return demonstration/t\neach-back correct.\nElectronically signed: Rachel Simmons, RN, BSN -   "system_note": "What was billed: Principal S36.032A (Major splenic laceration, MCC) with multiple MCC/CC comorbidities (including S72.302A - left femur shaft fracture, R57.01 cardiogenic shock, J95.851 VAP flagged POA=Y/CC), and 10 procedures including splenectomy (07TP0ZZ), endotracheal intubation (0BH17EZ), and prolonged ventilation (5A1D90Z).\n\nWhat the record actually documents and the audit decisions (evidence citations below):\n1) Principal diagnosis S36.032A (major splenic laceration, MCC) — KEEP as principal. Trauma H&P documents Grade IV splenic laceration with immediate OR splenectomy and IR embolization consistent with the Policy validation for a surgical/splenectomy pathway for S36.032A [ev1; ev2; ev3]. Policy explicitly lists S36.032A as AAST Grade III–V (MCC) and requires operative documentation or grade confirmation to support MCC assignment [ev15].\n2) Femur fracture side miscoding — RECODE S72.302A (left) -> S72.301A (right). Multiple contemporaneous clinical documents repeatedly identify a displaced mid-shaft RIGHT femur fracture and definitive right femoral intramedullary nailing (ICU day 4 / discharge summary), not a LEFT femur shaft fracture; therefore the billed left-side code is incorrect and should be the right-side shaft fracture (S72.301A) [ev1; ev4].\n3) Ventilator-associated pneumonia (J95.851) — KEEP the diagnosis code but CORRECT its POA and severity. Infectious Diseases documents “VAP developing shortly after extubation with clinical and radiographic features” and the discharge summary documents “hospital-acquired methicillin-susceptible S. aureus ventilator-associated pneumonia treated with cefazolin” with culture-directed therapy (vancomycin stopped when MSSA identified; cefazolin used) [ev5; ev6; ev7]. The governing VAP policy explicitly designates J95.851 as an MCC-level VAP diagnosis and requires POA = N because VAP is, by definition, hospital-acquired; the policy language states J95.851 should always carry POA = N and defines the timing and clinical criteria required to support assignment [ev9; ev8]. The claim had J95.851 flagged POA=Y and CC — both are incorrect per record + policy; POA must be N and severity MCC.\n4) Acute kidney failure (N17.9) POA flag incorrect — KEEP diagnosis but CHANGE POA to Y. The admitting H&P lists “Rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury (KDIGO 2), non-dialysis-requiring” and trauma/ICU labs on admission show creatinine 3.73 mg/dL, consistent with AKI present at admission (POA = Y) rather than a new inpatient-onset AKI; the claim currently shows POA = N [ev10; ev11].\n5) Cardiogenic shock (R57.01) — REMOVE. The contemporaneous documentation attributes the patient’s shock physiology to hemorrhagic/traumatic shock (hypotension in field, massive transfusion protocol, hemorrhagic shock, splenic hemorrhage) and operative splenectomy for hemorrhage; there is no provider documentation of cardiogenic shock in the record. Because cardiogenic shock is not documented or supported, R57.01 is not valid for this encounter and should be removed [ev12; ev3].\n6) Procedure-level corrections: all operative and procedural lines are supported except one external-fixation-of-right-upper-femur line (0QH60BZ) — REMOVE 0QH60BZ. result.finding_category: POA flag wrong; Diagnosis lacks clinical support; CC/MCC severity misclassified; Incorrect side-coded diagnosis / sequencing
result.system_note: What was billed: Principal S36.032A (Major splenic laceration, MCC) with multiple MCC/CC comorbidities (including S72.302A - left femur shaft fracture, R57.01 cardiogenic shock, J95.851 VAP flagged POA=Y/CC), and 10 procedures including splenectomy (07TP0ZZ), endotracheal intubation (0BH17EZ), and prolonged ventilation (5A1D90Z). What the record actually documents and the audit decisions (evidence citations below): 1) Principal diagnosis S36.032A (major splenic laceration, MCC) - KEEP as principal. Trauma H&P documents Grade IV splenic laceration with immediate OR splenectomy and IR embolization consistent with the Policy validation for a surgical/splenectomy pathway for S36.032A [ev1; ev2; ev3]. Policy explicitly lists S36.032A as AAST Grade III-V (MCC) and requires operative documentation or grade confirmation to support MCC assignment [ev15]. 2) Femur fracture side miscoding - RECODE S72.302A (left) -> S72.301A (right). Multiple contemporaneous clinical documents repeatedly identify a displaced mid-shaft RIGHT femur fracture and definitive right femoral intramedullary nailing (ICU day 4 / discharge summary), not a LEFT femur shaft fracture; therefore the billed left-side code is incorrect and should be the right-side shaft fracture (S72.301A) [ev1; ev4]. 3) Ventilator-associated pneumonia (J95.851) - KEEP the diagnosis code but CORRECT its POA and severity. Infectious Diseases documents "VAP developing shortly after extubation with clinical and radiographic features" and the discharge summary documents "hospital-acquired methicillin-susceptible S. aureus ventilator-associated pneumonia treated with cefazolin" with culture-directed therapy (vancomycin stopped when MSSA identified; cefazolin used) [ev5; ev6; ev7]. The governing VAP policy explicitly designates J95.851 as an MCC-level VAP diagnosis and requires POA = N because VAP is, by definition, hospital-acquired; the policy language states J95.851 should always carry POA = N and defines the timing and clinical criteria required to support assignment [ev9; ev8]. The claim had J95.851 flagged POA=Y and CC - both are incorrect per record + policy; POA must be N and severity MCC. 4) Acute kidney failure (N17.9) POA flag incorrect - KEEP diagnosis but CHANGE POA to Y. The admitting H&P lists "Rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury (KDIGO 2), non-dialysis-requiring" and trauma/ICU labs on admission show creatinine 3.73 mg/dL, consistent with AKI present at admission (POA = Y) rather than a new inpatient-onset AKI; the claim currently shows POA = N [ev10; ev11]. 5) Cardiogenic shock (R57.01) - REMOVE. The contemporaneous documentation attributes the patient's shock physiology to hemorrhagic/traumatic shock (hypotension in field, massive transfusion protocol, hemorrhagic shock, splenic hemorrhage) and operative splenectomy for hemorrhage; there is no provider documentation of cardiogenic shock in the record. Because cardiogenic shock is not documented or supported, R57.01 is not valid for this encounter and should be removed [ev12; ev3]. 6) Procedure-level corrections: all operative and procedural lines are supported except one external-fixation-of-right-upper-femur line (0QH60BZ) - REMOVE 0QH60BZ. The record documents pelvic external fixation and right femoral intramedullary nailing (pelvis ex-fix, IM nail of right femur). The orthopedic consultation and discharge/operative course describe external fixation of the pelvis and IM nailing of the right femur; there is no operative documentation that external fixation was placed on the right femur itself, so 0QH60BZ (external fixation of right upper femur) appears unsupported by the operative/course documentation and should be removed; the pelvic external fixator code (0SH90BZ) and right femur IM fixation (0QQ606Z) remain supported [ev4; ev3]. 7) Ventilator duration/procedure 5A1D90Z - KEEP. The discharge summary documents successful extubation on ICU day 9 (i.e. >96 hours of mechanical ventilation) and the chart shows continued mechanical ventilation and ICU therapy consistent with billing this prolonged-ventilation assistance code [ev13; ev2]. Summary of audit actions: remove unsupported cardiogenic-shock diagnosis (R57.01) and unsupported procedure 0QH60BZ; recode left femur shaft (S72.302A) to right-side (S72.301A); change POA and severity flags for J95.851 (POA from Y -> N; CC -> MCC) and change POA for N17.9 (N -> Y). All other billed diagnoses/procedures are supported and retained. Key evidence (document/section/page): see evidence_cited list below (ev1-ev15).
